These results suggest that techno-optimistic worldviews within science may inadvertently constrain the behavioral and cultural shifts required for effective climate action.

articles.title: How and why to read (and write and publish) academic research
articles.authors: Patrick E. Savage
articles.abstract: This article is designed to concisely teach undergraduate and new graduate students lessons in reading and writing I have learned in my past two decades as a university student, teacher, and researcher (including through publishing, retracting, correcting, and republishing articles in outlets with varying levels of “impact” and publication fees). Don’t just start at the beginning of an academic article/book and try to read straight to the end! Instead, I recommend starting by reading the title(s)/author(s) and abstract(s), then the figures, reading the Discussion section, and skimming/spot-checking the references, peer reviews, and data (e.g., spreadsheets, audiovisual stimuli, surveys), if available. Only once you have done this and evaluated whether it seems worth your time do I recommend deciding whether to read every word of some/all sections/chapters (and any accompanying supplementary material) or digging deeper into reanalysing/replicating the data. I recommend writing accordingly so that most of your key information will be conveyed even if your reader only gets through your title, abstract, and figures. I discuss various strategies to improve your own academic reading/writing and the broader culture of academia, from practical (e.g., formatting and tracking references and citations using Zotero and Google Scholar, asking constructive questions rather than self-promoting comments, publishing using Peer Community In Registered Reports, using the “sandwich thesis” model for PhD dissertations) to philosophical (e.g., ethical issues in authorship, citation, AI, publishing, and funding). I explain the intended goals of academic research (to create and distribute valuable new knowledge) and perverse incentives that lead us astray from these goals (e.g., chasing prestige and funding). I conclude by contemplating if and how we should dismantle the current extortionary academic-industrial complex and re-design it to align with its intended goals.

articles.title: Seeing without understanding: The late emergence of attentiveness as a basis for social evaluation
articles.authors: Shengyi Wu; Laura Schulz
articles.abstract: Children depend on attentive caregivers and track others’ attention starting in infancy. Strikingly however, four- and five-year-olds, unlike older children, do not expect other people to prefer attentive to distracted social partners (Exps 1-3), and do not selectively identify interventions likely to engage a social partner’s attention (Exp 4). By contrast, four- and five-year-olds have no difficulty recognizing that people will prefer social partners who fulfill (versus override) their desires (Exp 5); no difficulty using differences in others’ visual attention to infer what they do and do not know (Exp 6), and no difficulty using differences in others’ visual attention to distinguish attentive and distracted social partners (Exp 7). These results suggest that young children’s failure to understand the social value of attention is not due to task demands or a failure to track and understand visual attention. Rather, the results suggest a dissociation between young children’s sensitivity to others’ visual attention and their tendency to treat others’ attentiveness as relevant to social evaluation. This opens up new questions about a possible shift in children’s understanding of attention from representing it primarily as a perceptual phenomenon to understanding attention as a means of focusing limited cognitive resources.

articles.title: How to discover the natural kind of consciousness – and test for its presence – under population shifts
articles.authors: Megan A. K. Peters
articles.abstract:
Debates about artificial consciousness are often framed in terms of verdicts: whether a given system is or is not conscious, and which criteria or theories can deliver such judgments. This paper argues that this framing obscures a more fundamental epistemic challenge. Consciousness science has largely been developed within a narrow population – humans – under background assumptions that support evidential generalization within that domain but do not automatically extend to nonhuman animals or artificial systems. When our line of research expands to assess new populations that differ radically in embodiment, internal organization, and implementation, the central problem should be not only detection but also discovery: whether there even exists a stable cluster of properties that can support explanation and generalization across heterogeneous systems, which we might then call “consciousness”.
Here, I build on the iterative natural-kind (INK) strategy proposed by Bayne and Shea (2020) (see also (Bayne et al., 2024a, 2024b)) to lay out a roadmap for a proximity-guided extension of this approach. The INK strategy treats consciousness as a candidate natural kind whose structure is to be discovered through iterative revision of indicators, mappings between those indicators and the “natural kind” of consciousness, and the underlying natural kind itself. However, in its abstract form, INK leaves open how evidential updates should be accomplished under population shift. The present paper argues that proximity relations – to be understood as multidimensional similarities and differences between systems (Peters, n.d.) – provide the missing structure. By conditioning belief updates on explicit judgments about proximity within a Bayesian latent variable discovery model, a proximity-guided INK strategy renders several potential limitations of the INK strategy as visible, interrogable features such that they themselves can be objects of scientific investigation. The result is a methodological roadmap for investigating consciousness under uncertainty, focused not only on delivering verdicts but also on clarifying what kinds of discovery about the natural kind of “consciousness” may be possible.

articles.title: The time course of neural activity predictive of self-initiated movement
articles.authors: Lucas Jeay-Bizot; Mehmet Basbug; Uri Maoz; Robert Schapire; Aaron Schurger
articles.abstract: Decades of research have shown that early ramping activity is a very reliable antecedent of self-initiated movement. However, the dominant paradigm has been to only analyze data epochs culminating in movement, which discounts how often slow ramping might occur when no movement follows. To address this, we introduced a matched control condition that did not culminate in movement. We recorded electroencephalography data and compared these two conditions using a variety of powerful machine-learning classifiers. Although early ramping activity was present, it did not predict movement. Instead, classification accuracy rose abruptly about 100 ms before movement. By contrast, the traditional approach reproduced the spurious impression of early predictability. Our results resolve a long-standing controversy, showing that the neural commitment to act is a late-stage event consistent with the timing of conscious intention and the ability to inhibit movement. More broadly, our results show that a reliable antecedent is not necessarily a good predictor, underscoring the need for proper control conditions in time series analyses.

articles.title: Beyond the phenomenology of innocence: An exploratory study of innocent suspects’ reasoning about the disclosure of critical information in an investigative interviewing context
articles.authors: Helen Wyler; Natalie Harrison
articles.abstract: Contemporary guidelines on effective investigative interviewing encourage strategic approaches to disclosing evidence, such as the Strategic Use of Evidence (SUE) technique. The SUE is grounded in research suggesting that innocent and guilty suspects manage information differently during interviews, with innocent suspects generally being more forthcoming, including about potentially self-incriminating information. Innocent suspects’ forthcomingness is often attributed to the phenomenology of innocence (PoI), yet direct empirical evidence remains limited, and little is known about innocent suspects’ underlying reasoning. We conducted semi-structured interviews with 12 participants who imagined being wrongfully suspected of theft and analysed their accounts using reflexive thematic analysis from a critical realist perspective. Eleven participants indicated they would be completely truthful in the hypothetical police interview, but expectations of being believed varied. Three themes were identified: (i) beliefs about truthfulness and the recognisability of innocence, (ii) reasoning about credibility in light of evidence, and (iii) anticipated personal, social, and situational influences on credibility judgements. Several participants believed that honesty would convey innocence, consistent with PoI-related reasoning. However, participants also considered how evidence, burden of proof, social perception, and situational interpretation might affect their credibility. These findings suggest that PoI may be only one component of a broader evaluative process guiding innocent suspects’ anticipated disclosure decisions. We propose subjective expected utility as a testable framework that may help identify conditions under which innocent suspects may disclose less. If supported, this perspective may provide a more differentiated understanding of innocent suspects’ decision-making and ultimately help identify potential high-risk constellations in practice.

articles.title: Understanding stakeholders’ views on 24-hour movement behaviours in early childhood in Scotland
articles.authors: Jessica John; Hollie Miller; Deirdre Harrington; Xanne Janssen; Paul Flowers; Brad MacDonald; Marion Henderson; Farid Bardid
articles.abstract:
Background: The early years are a critical window for establishing healthy 24-hour movement behaviours, encompassing physical activity, sedentary behaviour (including screen time), and sleep. Stakeholder views are essential for understanding the multilevel barriers and enablers to promoting 24-hour movement behaviours that benefit health, as they are ultimately responsible for the dissemination and implementation of guidelines and interventions.
Methods: Data were collected in 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic restrictions. A qualitative design was used, consisting of semi-structured focus groups (n = 4) with stakeholders (n = 18). This included researchers, public health professionals, and individuals from the private sector and third sector organisations. Focus group data were analysed using a codebook thematic analysis.
Results: Stakeholders discussed (1) their desire for a shared holistic vision for early years movement – agreeing that physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep are interconnected across the 24-hour day and calling for the early years to be centred in multisector collaborations; (2) the complexity of communicating guidance on 24-hour movement behaviours clearly and without stigma; (3) the central role of community and informal networks in communicating guidelines and supporting 24-hour movement behaviours; (4) the constraint realities of family life in determining what families can realistically do regardless of what guidelines recommend; (5) hidden determinants of behaviours including adult mental health, relational well-being and social economic inequalities; and (6) structural barriers such as policy fragmentation, under investment in early-years services, geographical inequalities, and lasting disruptions of the COVID-19 restrictions.
Conclusion: Stakeholders understood 24-hour movement behaviours in early childhood as shaped by interacting influences across the levels of the socio-ecological model (intrapersonal, interpersonal, community, institutional and public policy). Effective communication requires a coordinated, multi-level response that addresses structural barriers and systemic inequalities, supports families as actors in constrained circumstances, and moves beyond approaches that place the burden of change solely at the intrapersonal level.

articles.title: When Threats Backfire: Overcharged Defendants Overestimate Their Trial Prospects and Reject Plea Offers More Often
articles.authors: Stephanie Aurora Cárdenas
articles.abstract:
Objectives: Overcharging involves threatening disproportionately harsh punishment to widen the discount between the potential sentence if convicted at trial (PTS) and the plea offer sentence. Though larger discounts increase plea acceptance, PTSs can counterintuitively reduce acceptances when discounts are held proportionally constant. Drawing on anchoring theories, I investigate whether this independent effect of PTS reflects distinct processing pathways: lower elaboration influences primarily on maximum acceptable plea sentence, and/or higher elaboration influences on case appraisals (e.g., perceived evidence strength and conviction likelihood).
Hypotheses: In Experiments 1a and 1b, I predicted that (a) transparently case-irrelevant anchors, used as a stringent test of low-elaboration influence, would not affect plea decisions. In Experiment 2, I predicted that (b) a relevant, disproportionately harsh PTS would increase maximum acceptable plea sentences; and (c) higher sentencing preferences would increase plea acceptances. 
Method: Prolific adults read a felony-DUI vignette and rendered a plea decision. Experiments 1a (N = 247) and 1b (N = 193) tested whether irrelevant anchors (48 vs. 8 months to graduate veterinary school) influence plea decisions when procedures discourage treating them as informative. Experiment 2 (N = 844) tested whether a more consequential, case-relevant PTS (18 vs. 4 years vs. none) would promote higher elaboration by altering case appraisals, maximum sentencing preferences, and, in turn, plea decisions.
Results: Contrasting prior work, irrelevant anchors did not alter plea acceptances, ORExperiment_1a = 0.95 [0.57, 1.57]; ORExperiment_1b = 1.01 [0.56, 1.80]. In Experiment 2, a disproportionately harsh PTS increased maximum sentencing preferences (d18_vs_4 = 1.04 [0.87, 1.22]; d18_vs_No_PTS = 0.75 [0.58, 0.92]), but, paradoxically, increased estimates of acquittal (OR18_vs_4 = 1.74 [1.25, 2.44]; OR18_vs_No_PTS = 1.56 [1.12, 2.18]), strengthened perceptions of favorable evidence (d18_vs_4 = 0.26 [0.09, 0.42]; d18_vs_No_PTS = 0.22 [0.06, 0.39]), and decreased plea acceptances when compared to a less extreme PTS (OR18_vs_4 = 0.5 [0.32, 0.79]).
Conclusions: PTS may influence acceptances through distinct pathways—altering maximum sentencing preferences through less thoughtful processes, but case appraisals via more thoughtful processes. This challenges the rational actor shadow-of-the-trial model assumption that treats PTS and conviction likelihood as independent, exogenous inputs to defendants’ plea decisions. Practically, overcharging may backfire from its intended strategic goal by causing defendants to overestimate their trial prospects.

articles.title: Towards automating the harmonization of diverse mental health scales: a comparison of large language models and human judgements
articles.authors: Bettina Moltrecht; Thomas Wood; Rachel Holland Gomes; Rebecca Louise Quinn; Caitlyn Rawers; Mark Shevlin; Maurice D Mulvenna; Raymond Bond; Eoin McElroy
articles.abstract: Combining existing mental health datasets offers considerable value, making it possible to answer new research questions, increase statistical power, and replicate findings across different populations. However, a barrier to this process is that different research teams often use different measures/scales when collecting mental health data and when monitoring or measuring patient/participant outcomes. This study examined whether large language models (LLMs) can support retrospective harmonisation of questionnaire data by identifying semantically and conceptually similar items across different scales. A sample of 92 volunteers rated the conceptual similarity of randomly allocated pairs of mental health questionnaire items on a scale from 0 (completely unrelated) to 100 (identical), producing 2,729 item-pair ratings. These ratings were compared with cosine similarity scores for each item-pair, generated by three LLM-based approaches. Linear regression models indicated that cosine similarity scores positively predicted human similarity ratings, with standardised coefficients ranging from β = 0.27 to β = 0.39. However, 10-fold cross-validation indicated limited predictive accuracy when estimating human ratings from cosine scores. Receiver operating characteristic analyses were therefore used to examine whether cosine scores could support threshold-based screening of candidate item pairs. Using binary judgements of whether participants rated item pairs as similar, a cosine similarity threshold of approximately 0.31 provided the best overall balance between sensitivity and specificity. Applied to the present item battery (i.e. manually reviewing item-pairs with a cosine of 0.31 or greater), this threshold would have reduced the number of item-pairs requiring review by approximately 69%. These findings suggest that LLM-derived similarity scores may help make retrospective harmonisation more efficient and replicable by reducing the burden of manual screening. However, the modest predictive performance observed here indicates that LLM outputs should be used to prioritise candidate item pairs for expert review rather than as standalone indicators of item equivalence. Further fine-tuning, validation, and replication across broader sets of constructs and questionnaires are required.

articles.title: Debunking decreases mistaken causal inferences: A direct replication of Irving et al. (2022)
articles.authors: Dhruv Aggarwal; Keyi Zhang; James Edward Bartlett
articles.abstract: We conducted a direct replication of Irving et al. (2022) examining whether a debunking statement reduces mistaken causal inferences from correlational evidence. We randomly allocated participants to read a news article containing either a correction statement (n = 65) or a no-correction control (n = 64). Participants in the correction group made fewer causal inferences (delta = 0.65, 95% HDI [0.30, 1.00]) and more correlational inferences (delta = 0.72, 95% HDI [0.36, 1.07]) compared to the no correction group. In exploratory analyses, we also supported the robustness of their findings to alternative modelling choices. Our findings represent a successful direct replication of Irving et al.

articles.title: Alternative explanations of associations between birth experiences, rumination, and postpartum depressive symptoms: A comment on Aker et al. (2026)
articles.authors: Kimmo Sorjonen; Bo Melin; Marika Melin
articles.abstract: Aker et al. concluded that birth experiences, measured by self-rated degree of traumatic child birth and birth satisfaction, had an impact on postpartum depressive symptoms and that this effect was mediated by rumination. Here, we fitted alternative models to the same covariance structure and these models suggested, instead, that associations could be due to a negative effect of a latent general vulnerability factor on birth satisfaction. This is an example of a common situation where competing conclusions are underdetermined by the available data. We recommend researchers to fit alternative models to their data, compare findings, and to think more deeply about what conclusions the data really can be claimed to support.

articles.title: Subjective mental imagery vividness and objective accuracy predict chess performance
articles.authors: Stephen M Emrich; Benjamin Balas
articles.abstract: Despite its theoretical importance to performance, it remains an open empirical question whether stronger chess players experience more vivid mental imagery. We recruited an online sample of 44 chess players, spanning a wide range of skill levels, who completed imagery questionnaires and an objective probe task requiring identification of the color of a square on an imagined chessboard. Both subjective imagery vividness and probe accuracy were positively associated with chess skill. Stronger players were also more likely to adopt visualization strategies over non-visual strategies, and were more likely to endorse looking away from the board while solving a chess problem. Critically, vividness of imagery during chess problem-solving predicted skill both directly and indirectly. That is, more vivid imagery predicted stronger performance even when accounting for its effect on strategy preference. Among three self-reported aphantasics, one high-skilled player nonetheless performed comparably to the full sample on the probe task, placing in the top 10% of the sample overall, and uniquely reported imagery vividness only when the board was visible. These findings suggest that the vividness of mental imagery contributes to chess performance, in part by shaping which cognitive strategies players use to approach the game, while also indicating that mental imagery vividness is not a strict requirement for expertise.

articles.title: Migration, Environment, and the Brain: A Systematic Synthesis of Evidence
articles.authors: Izabela Maria Sztuka; Jiaona Hu; Simone Kühn
articles.abstract:
Migration—a defining process in human development—is a profound contemporary challenge involving hundreds of millions of people every year. The process exposes individuals to profound biosocial challenges connected to heightened risk of psychiatric disorders and decreased mental well-being. To date, this risk has been understood largely within a framework of socio-cultural factors, such as acculturative stress, discrimination, and socioeconomic adversity. Here we propose to broaden this scope by incorporating the physical environmental and neurobiological dimensions of migration, which remain comparatively underexplored despite recent advances in environmental neuroscience.
For this purpose, we conducted a systematic synthesis of evidence at the intersection of migration, environment, and neurobiology, pre-registered on the Open Science Framework and reported according to PRISMA 2020. Searches of PubMed, PsycINFO, and Scopus yielded 16,910 unique records, from which 94 studies (1989–2026, 19 countries) met inclusion criteria: 64 (68%) environment-focused, 21 (22%) brain-focused, and 9 (10%) integrating both.
Environment-focused studies showed that neighborhood deprivation, segregation, and social fragmentation were consistently linked to poorer mental health, while green/blue space access and neighborhood cohesion were often protective; urbanicity showed inconsistent associations. Brain-focused studies, concentrated in trauma-exposed refugees, implicated fronto-limbic and large-scale network systems in threat processing, emotion regulation, and stress-sensitive neurobiology, but rarely measured physical environmental exposure directly. The few studies integrating environment and neurobiology centered on extreme exposures—high-altitude relocation, war-related toxicants, occupational pesticides—demonstrating that environmental embedding in the migrant brain is empirically tractable, while leaving everyday environmental transitions (housing, urbanicity, pollution, green space) unexamined at the neurobiological level.
Together, these findings suggest that migration-related vulnerability is not a fixed property of migrant status itself but is shaped by the environmental conditions of movement and settlement. We propose a neuroecological research agenda that reframes the central question from whether migrants differ from non-migrants to which environmental transitions, for whom, and under what conditions, foster adaptation, vulnerability, or resilience.

articles.title: The influence of glucose intake and psychosocial stress on food craving in healthy adults
articles.authors: Flora Nasilowski; Julia Reichenberger; Bernadette Denk; Raphaela Gaertner; Elea S. C. Klink; Eva Unternaehrer; Nina Volkmer; Stella Wienhold; Jens C Pruessner; Maria Meier
articles.abstract:
Stress has been linked to the consumption of palatable food and may contribute to the development of obesity. Interindividual differences in cortisol stress reactivity are discussed as mediating mechanisms, yet findings linking food craving to cortisol reactivity are heterogeneous. Methodological differences in whether participants receive a sugary preload or are invited fasted may contribute to these divergences. Hence, this study set out to systematically investigate the effect of glucose and psychosocial stress on food craving in healthy adults. 
Overall, 62 healthy, fasted adults (mean age = 23.13; SD = 3.02; 54.84 % female, 45.16 % male) reported current food craving on the Food Craving Questionnaire, received either glucose or water and were later exposed to psychosocial stress or a friendly control condition. After stressor exposure, food craving was assessed a second time. We repeatedly assessed salivary cortisol and blood glucose and used linear mixed models to test whether the experimental manipulations predicted changes in craving and explored associations with sex and stress-eating tendency.
Blood glucose increased in those consuming glucose and the stress test increased cortisol significantly. Higher cortisol reactivity, and even stronger, a greater increase in blood glucose led to significant reductions in food craving over time. We found no supportive evidence that glucose and cortisol reactivity interactively affected craving. 
These findings suggest that short-term metabolic signals may be more influential in shaping immediate food craving than acute stress, and that acute cortisol elevations may not universally promote food craving.

articles.title: Making Cooperation Comparable: Conditional Response Profiles as a Common Currency for Cross-Species Cooperation Research
articles.authors: Sophie Siestrup; Ricarda Ines Schubotz; Helene Richter; Yves Breitmoser
articles.abstract: Cooperation is widespread across species, but comparative research is limited by the difficulty of measuring the same cooperative problem in humans and non-human animals. We propose the iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma (IPD) as a controlled framework for studying repeated, partner-contingent cooperation across species. The central requirement is not that all species use the same apparatus, but that they face the same repeated social contingency through species-appropriate interfaces. We argue that overall cooperation rates are insufficient for such comparisons, because similar rates can arise from different behavioural processes. Instead, comparative IPD studies should estimate conditional response profiles: initial cooperation and the probability of cooperation after mutual cooperation, asymmetric outcomes, and mutual noncooperation. Drawing on human repeated-game experiments, animal cooperation studies, and theoretical work on repeated-game strategies, we derive design and reporting principles for cross-species IPD research. These include implementing a credible payoff ranking, calibrating reward value within each species, ensuring identifiable partners and repeated dyadic interaction, reporting state coverage, and treating strategy labels as behavioural summaries rather than claims about mental representation. The proposed framework is intended to complement, not replace, ecological studies of cooperation. It provides a formal bridge between controlled laboratory designs and species-specific social systems, allowing researchers to ask whether similar conditional patterns of cooperation emerge across different evolutionary and cognitive contexts.

articles.title: Self-prioritisation in arbitrary shape-label associations is not sufficient to distort duration perception
articles.authors: Irena Arslanova; Manos Tsakiris
articles.abstract: How we perceive time is shaped by attention and emotion, but more recent work suggests that information related to one’s self can also expand subjective time. However, previous self-relevance manipulations have been confounded with familiarity, affective meaning, or embodiment. Across three online experiments, we tested whether minimal self-relevance created through arbitrary shape-label associations was sufficient to bias duration perception. Participants learned that geometric shapes referred to themselves, a stranger, and, in Experiments 2 and 3, a friend. They then completed a non-temporal task probing the learned associations, followed by a duration bisection task in which they estimated the duration of the associated shapes. The non-temporal tasks produced robust self-prioritisation: self-associated shapes were processed faster and more accurately than stranger-associated shapes, with evidence for a graded self–friend–stranger pattern in Experiments 2 and 3. Yet self-association did not produce the predicted temporal expansion. A small increase in temporal precision for self-associated shapes in Experiment 1 did not replicate, and pooled analyses showed only very small temporal effects. These findings suggest a distinction between minimal, task-instructed self-associations that can bias non-temporal decisions and richer forms of self-relevance that may be needed to shape time experience.

articles.title: Retroactive Facilitation and Change Awareness Across Lags and Retention Intervals
articles.authors: Christopher N. Wahlheim; Geoff Ward; Samuel W. Cox
articles.abstract: Memory for an earlier event can be impaired by later studying a related event (retroactive interference). However, when later events cue retrievals of earlier events that also enable integrative encoding, memory for the earlier event can be enhanced (retroactive facilitation). Two experiments using continuous A-B, A-C paired-associate tasks examined retroactive memory effects across lags and retention intervals. We indexed study-phase retrieval and integrative encoding by examining associations between awareness of changes and memory for first responses. Participants studied A-B, A-C, and retention-interval-matched A-B pairs and indicated when they detected response changes. The lag between A-B and A-C and the retention interval between A-C and test trials varied factorially across 4, 16, and 48 intervening items. Cued-recall test formats differed: Experiment 1 prompted direct retrieval of first responses, with participants reporting recollected changes. Experiment 2 used modified-modified free recall in which participants reported responses as they came to mind and indicated whether they were the first, second, or only responses; the first two decisions indicated recollection of changes. Both experiments showed the greatest retroactive facilitation at the longest retention interval and intermediate lag. Retroactive facilitation co-occurred with and was statistically associated with detection and recollection of changes, suggesting these processes contributed to the observed effect. Negatively curvilinear, non-monotonic lag functions occurred for A-B, A-C recall at the longest retention interval and were associated with detected changes, especially those not recollected. These findings may be accounted for by a memory-for-change framework with a role for contextual variability that determines study-phase retrieval success.

articles.title: Is gender truly stable? Longitudinal changes in gender identity in a Dutch community sample
articles.authors: Jessie Hillekens; Fernando Salinas-Quiroz; Lysanne te Brinke
articles.abstract: Gender has been conceptualized as a stable individual trait in developmental psychology. Consequently, little is known about potential gender identity changes in adolescence and early adulthood. This study explored 1) whether and how frequent changes in gender identity occur and 2) what these changes look like. Using eight-wave longitudinal data, Dutch youth (N=933; Mage=18.72, SD=3.73) reported their gender identity repeatedly. Results showed that approximately one out of 20 youth changed their gender identity at least once, with several changing multiple times during the study. Whereas some youth changed between binary options (i.e., boy/man or girl/woman), others (also) considered nonbinary identities – either by identifying as such or through various self-descriptions. Youth also used other ways to communicate potential gender-expansiveness, including self-describe, ‘prefer not to say’ and missing data patterns. Our findings highlight gender identity as dynamic and contextual construct that continues to change beyond childhood and should be recognized as such.

articles.title: Art of Living for Teachers: A Training to Enhance Well-Being and Reduce Stress
articles.authors: Febe Findeis; Julian Duhm; Mira Schwarz
articles.abstract: Teachers are at high risk of burnout and various occupational stressors, making preventive measures to promote their well-being highly important. Since studies on the effectiveness of the Art-of-Living approach among teachers are currently lacking, this study addresses that research gap. In a randomized controlled design with three groups and three measurement points, N = 158 teachers are assigned to an experimental group with individual exercises (EG1), a combined group with individual and environmental exercises (EG2), and an active placebo control group (CG). The seven-day intervention is based on the Art-of-Living repertoire and is designed as a Wise-Intervention. To assess well-being and burnout, the PANAS, SWLS, AOLI, and CBI are used. The two-way repeated measures ANOVA shows no significant group × time interaction. However, t-tests for dependent measures reveal significant reductions in Negative Affect and burnout scores in EG1 with moderate effect sizes. In EG2, only a significant reduction in Negative Affect is observed, whereas delayed effects on burnout and Art-of-Living become visible only in the follow-up measurement. The effects observed remain stable from post-measurement to follow-up, and there are no significant differences between the two experimental groups. The findings provide initial promising evidence that the Art-of-Living approach is suitable as a low-threshold, everyday preventive measure to promote teachers' well-being. Future studies should employ longer intervention periods, larger sample sizes, and additional measurement tools to substantiate the effectiveness of this approach further.

articles.title: CLDassist: LLM-assisted CLD construction
articles.authors: Meike Waaijers; Hannes Rosenbusch; Caspar J. Van Lissa; Anne Roefs; Denny Borsboom
articles.abstract: The Causal Loop Diagram (CLD) method is a structured approach for constructing conceptual representations of how variables may causally relate to one another, developed either individually or collaboratively with a group of experts. However, CLD construction is labor-intensive, time-consuming, and cognitively demanding. Large Language Models (LLMs), with their advanced text processing capabilities and extensive knowledge base, offer the potential to support this process. This paper presents CLDassist, an R package and Shiny app that supports CLD construction by integrating LLMs into the CLD construction process. Researchers can use CLDassist to define a list of putative variables, then query an LLM to evaluate causal links between these variables and provide supporting literature. Rather than replacing expert judgment, CLDassist functions as a thinking partner that helps researchers explore causal relationships and organize causal structures. We describe how LLMs can be used to assist in the CLD construction process and demonstrate empirically that the agreement between CLDassist and human experts is comparable to the agreement observed between experts themselves. In addition to helping researchers generate an initial CLD, CLDassist may reduce tunnel vision in the modeling process by suggesting alternative perspectives and highlighting variables or relationships that may otherwise be overlooked. By combining the established CLD method with the generative capabilities of LLMs, CLDassist provides users with a standardized, multi-stage framework for supporting the early stages of theory formalization.

articles.title: Are mathematics anxiety and being positive about mathematics mutually exclusive? An exploratory study in elite STEM students
articles.authors: Venera Gashaj; Vera R. Baumgartner; Serena Rossi; Alexander von Bergen; Hannah Connolly; Manu Kapur; Krzysztof Cipora
articles.abstract: Mathematics Anxiety (MA) has been studied mainly in heterogeneous samples and in students with mathematical difficulties, whereas elite STEM students remain largely understudied. This neglect is partly based on the assumption that choosing mathematics-intensive programmes implies uniformly positive attitudes toward mathematics. In the present study, we investigated MA and related constructs in a large sample of elite STEM students (N ≈ 4,600) at a leading technical university, comparing students across mathematics-light, mathematics-heavy, and pure-mathematics programmes and across different stages of study. Overall, MA was lower than in reference samples but showed substantial individual variation. MA followed a clear gradient across programmes and was higher in first-year students than in more advanced students. Exploratory factor analysis identified nine internally consistent factors that distinguished mathematics-specific constructs from language-related and general anxiety-related factors. Latent profile analyses further revealed distinct patterns of anxiety and, critically, profiles in which elevated MA co-occurred with strong positive mathematical experiences, particularly among pure-mathematics students. Together, these findings show that anxiety and positive engagement with mathematics are not mutually exclusive in elite STEM populations. They highlight the need for a differentiated understanding of MA and for targeted support that strengthens self-efficacy and resilience while sustaining students’ engagement and well-being.

articles.title: Biased processing of multiple outcomes in human reinforcement learning: evidence from computational modeling and eye-tracking
articles.authors: Henri Vandendriessche; Gruson Charlotte; Antonios Nasioulas; Camille Straboni; Maël Lebreton; Stefano Palminteri
articles.abstract: In many circumstances, choices result in multiple simultaneous outcomes, all of which should be integrated to optimally update reward expectation. Yet, to date, empirical investigations of reinforcement learning have mostly focused on situations where choices deliver only one outcome at a time. To understand how humans learn from multiple outcomes, we designed a new reinforcement learning task, where the selection of an option resulted in two outcomes drawn from the same underlying distribution over potential gains and losses, even if ultimately only one of the two counted for the final payoff. Behavioral results show that the two - equally informative- outcomes are considered, yet asymmetrically as function of their valence. This behavioral observation is backed up by computational analyses showing that, on top of previously documented asymmetric update, multiple outcome integration is biased, such as it overweighs rewards over punishments. Behavioral and computational results were paralleled by eye-tracking analysis showing that attention deployment is biased by outcome valence and relevance. The main results were confirmed in a second experiment featuring complete feedback information. Overall, our findings suggest that, when options deliver multiple discordant outcomes, losses tend to be neglected compared to gains.

articles.title: Friendship in mind: linking mental representations of friendships to well-being
articles.authors: Feng-Chun Ben Chou; Chih-Yuan E. Chang; Wen-Ting W. Lee; Jen-Ho Chang; Pin-Hao Andy Chen
articles.abstract: Strong social connections fundamentally shape human well-being and influence how individuals interpret their world. While previous research highlights the importance of friendships for well-being, the role of mental representations of friendships remains less explored. Since friendships involve both cross-situational variability and multidimensional features, capturing their complexity requires approaches that move beyond single indicators of relationship quality or quantity. This study examined whether higher well-being is associated with greater similarity in mental representations of friendships across contexts, consistent with the Anna Karenina Principle. We developed a two-level friendship rating task to assess mental representations of friendships across different dimensions and contexts. Using rating task data from 1,190 participants, we applied intersubject correlation analysis to quantify similarity in mental representations of friendships. We then identified latent dimensions of friendship representations and tested which dimensions were significantly associated with well-being. We found that greater similarity in mental representations of friendships was associated with higher well-being. We then identified three friendship dimensions, including socio-emotional, instrumental, and collectivism, with only the socio-emotional dimension strongly linked to well-being. Our findings suggest that well-being is associated not only with friendships themselves, but also with how individuals mentally represent the socio-emotional aspect of friendships. Shared socio-emotional factors may be an important psychosocial factor linking social connectedness and mental health.

articles.title: The Linear Relationship Between Visual Imagery and Alexithymia Breaks When Imagery Is Absent: Complete Aphantasics Are No More Alexithymic Than Typical Imagers
articles.authors: Maël Delem; Marine MAS; Olivier Luminet; Gaën Plancher; Perrine RUBY
articles.abstract: Several studies have suggested a link between aphantasia (reduced or absent visual mental imagery) and alexithymia (difficulty identifying and describing one's feelings, together with an externally oriented thinking style), but results and interpretations differ across studies, and no consensus has emerged. We pooled data from five independent studies (N = 1478: 147 complete aphantasics, 141 hypophantasics, 1115 typical imagers, 75 hyperphantasics) who completed the Vividness of Visual Imagery Questionnaire and the twenty-item Toronto Alexithymia Scale, and compared six candidate models, from linear and categorical baselines to several non-linear alternatives (GAM, Segmented and Floor-group models), to determine the shape of the relationship between visual imagery vividness and alexithymia, rather than assuming it in advance. The best fitting and most interpretable model (floor-group) showed  that among all participants capable of some degree of visual imagery (from hypo- to hyperphantasics), alexithymia declined as visual imagery vividness increased, consistent across all three TAS-20 sub-scales. Complete aphantasics broke this linear relationship entirely: rather than showing the highest level of alexithymia, as the linear relationship would predict, their scores were lower than that of hypophantasics and did not meaningfully differ from those of typical imagers. This discontinuity, specific to the total absence of visual imagery, was corroborated by an equally well-fitting segmented model, held up across all five studies individually, and is inconsistent with prior work treating any degree of reduced imagery as equivalent. Our results support the idea that some components of alexithymia are related to the level of visual imagery vividness in people that experience visual imagery. However, in people with complete aphantasia, alexithymia levels may depend on other processes. In other words, having no visual imagery at all does not seem to be associated with increased alexithymia levels, while having very weak visual imagery does.

articles.title: PupilFear: benchmarking pupillometry methods for fear conditioning on a distributed dynamical database
articles.authors: Jurjen Heij; Sourav Kulkarni; Federico Mancinelli; Olivier de Vries; Dominik R Bach
articles.abstract: Behavioral science increasingly relies on complex, computational pipelines to infer latent psychological variables from time-series data. Because the same data can often be processed using multiple plausible approaches, analytic choices may substantially affect results, yet systematic method comparisons remain uncommon. Here, we adress this problem for pupillometric measurement of fear conditioning. We introduce M-BIDS, a constrained, machine-interpretable extension of the Brain Imaging Data Structure, together with a distributed dynamic database (DDDB) architecture for harmonizing source data stored across multiple repositories. Using this framework, we assembled PupilFear, comprising 361 pupillometry datasets from fear-acquisition experiments. We benchmarked more than 700 candidate measurement methods spanning alternative preprocessing and response-quantification choices. Performance was evaluated using retrodictive validity, and decision tree regression was used to identify the analytic decisions most strongly associated with performance. The distinction between condition- and trial-wise modelign was the dominant determinant of retrodictive validity. Condition-wise model-based approaches showed relatively stable performance across parameter settings, whereas trial-wise approaches were substantially more sensitive to preprocessing choices. Nevertheless, the best condition-wise and trial-wise methods achieved comparable retrodictive validity (d = 0.65). Methods also differed in their sensitivity to reinforced trials (US bias). Peak-scoring approaches showed lower retrodictive validity overall (d = 0.45) but were less influenced by reinforcement-related responses. These finding provide practical guidance for selecting pupillometry pipelines according to the research question. The publicly available PupilFear corpus and benchmarking workflow also enable researchers to reproduce the analyses and evaluate new methods against a common reference.

articles.title: Minimally counterintuitive traits predict the long-term popularity of modern fictional characters: A quantitative analysis of the original 151 Pokémon
articles.authors: Mao Koshimizu; Yo Nakawake; Masaki Suyama
articles.abstract: Minimally counterintuitive (MCI) theory has been proposed to explain common features inherent in supernatural, mythological, or religious concepts across diverse cultural traditions. According to this theory, these concepts often embody an optimal balance of counterintuitive elements, enhancing their cognitive attraction and likelihood of widespread transmission. While previous research has explored the prevalence of minimal counterintuitiveness in characters from traditional folklore, it remains to be investigated whether this theory can also be applicable to modern fictional characters. The present study investigates the presence of MCI traits in the original 151 Pokémon and how these traits relate to their long-term popularity. Our findings demonstrate that the majority of counterintuitive Pokémon exhibit a minimal number of violations, and MCI status significantly predicts their ranking in global popularity polls.

articles.title: Online Platforms Provide Access to Valid Eastern Samples
articles.authors: Liman Wang; Randy Gao; Minah H. Jung; Iris W. Hung; Leif D. Nelson
articles.abstract: Behavioral scientists make claims about humans, but most research relies on English-speaking Americans. Despite longstanding concerns about this narrow sampling, only limited progress has been made to address it. We evaluated Chinese online participant pools, a potentially valuable resource given China’s large population, global influence, and frequent comparison with Western societies. Across 16 preregistered studies covering 21 established phenomena from behavioral and cultural sciences, we collected data from 24,932 Chinese and American participants. Chinese online platforms produced data broadly comparable to established American platforms. Participants were geographically and demographically diverse, attentive, and showed high test–retest reliability and temporal stability. Psychological and cultural effects were robust to variation in translation and translator backgrounds. We also provide practical insights and guidance for researchers using Chinese online platforms. This work helps reduce logistical barriers to extending behavioral research beyond traditionally studied WEIRD populations.

articles.title: JEAM: A Framework and Tutorial for Applying Evidence Accumulation Models to Continuous Judgments
articles.authors: Amir Hosein Hadian Rasanan; Nathan J. Evans; Jörg Rieskamp
articles.abstract: Experimental paradigms using continuous-response scales are widely employed across cognitive psychology. Over the past decade, multi-dimensional diffusion decision models (MD-DDMs) have been developed to investigate the cognitive processes underlying continuous-response decisions. Although these models have successfully captured and explained behavioral regularities across a range of cognitive domains, their adoption in applied research remains limited. One major barrier is the lack of accessible and flexible computational tools for model estimation. In this work, we introduce and provide a tutorial on using JEAM, a Python package for evidence accumulation modeling of continuous judgments. JEAM provides a fast and numerically stable framework for likelihood-based estimation of MD-DDMs. Moreover, it supports a broad range of response formats, including one-dimensional bounded and wrapped scales, as well as two-dimensional planar scales. The package also supports diffusion models with time-varying decision thresholds and arbitrary threshold dynamics, enabling the modeling of decision urgency. In addition, JEAM allows users to implement regression-like mapping functions that modulate model parameters as a function of experimental conditions, stimulus properties, or auxiliary variables such as neural activity. The package further supports mixture-process modeling, which is commonly used in judgment studies. Together, JEAM provides a flexible computational framework for modeling decision processes in continuous judgment tasks.

articles.title: Psychosocial profiles of pandemic and health emergency preparedness: a latent class analysis across four European countries
articles.authors: Catarina Santos Ribeiro; Mart van Dijk; Maartje Boer; Helena Jeriček Klanšček; Aaron Deegan; Heber Rowan; Maria Falcon; Maria Romay-Barja; Marina Šinko; Maruša Rehberger
articles.abstract: Societal resilience during health emergencies relies, in addition to healthcare capacity and infrastructure, on citizen wellbeing, social cohesion and collective behaviour. The latter dimensions are often under-addressed in preparedness planning. To address this, we used a Latent class analysis to identify psychosocial and behavioural preparedness profiles from the March 2024 Pandemic and Emergency Preparedness and Behaviour survey conducted in Ireland, the Netherlands, Slovenia and Spain (N=4,636). Three broad profiles emerged with relative consistency across countries: a Priority Support Group with low personal (mental health, resilience and social support) and societal (institutional trust and social cohesion) resources; an Individually Prepared Group with high personal resources; and a Collectively Prepared Group with high societal resources. Key determinants driving group memberships varied between countries, especially mental health, resilience and institutional trust. Young adults, women and people with lower education, living alone or with medical conditions were consistently more likely to belong to the Priority Support Group. We conclude that population variance in preparedness profiles was predominantly shaped by psychosocial resources rather than behaviours, highlighting the need for tailored interventions addressing personal and societal shortcomings by population profiles. Preparedness strategies should move beyond behavioural messaging and address psychosocial conditions that shape whether people can prepare.

articles.title: Does mindfulness reduce automatic preference development?
articles.authors: Brendan Hutchinson; Joanna Kuczynska; Julia Udden; Stephen Whitmarsh; Heleen A Slagter
articles.abstract:
Objectives. Trait mindfulness—one’s disposition toward non-judgmental awareness of present-moment experience—has been associated with various affective and cognitive outcomes. One proposed mechanism is that this kind of mindfulness attenuates the tendency to become attached to some experiences and avoid others. In line with this, a previous study reported that trait mindfulness reduced the development of affective preferences for letter strings that, unbeknownst to participants (n=18), followed a specific grammatical structure (Whitmarsh et al., 2013). If robust, this finding would confirm that trait mindfulness reduces implicit affective biases. In this pre-registered study, we aimed to replicate this main finding with a much larger sample size (n=127) and also explored whether prior meditation experience influenced implicit preference formation.
Methods. Trait mindfulness was measured in 127 participants using the Five-Facet Mindfulness Questionnaire (Baer, 2011). Over five days, participants were exposed to strings of apparently random letters, some of which conformed to an artificial grammar. They reproduced these strings in a working memory task and later rated whether they liked them, providing an index of implicit preference.
Results. We replicated basic artificial grammar learning effects but found no association between trait mindfulness and implicit preference development. Meditation experience similarly showed no effect on preference formation.
Conclusion. In this preregistered study, we did not replicate the previously reported effect of trait mindfulness on implicit preferences with our larger sample and improved design. Preference development may be too automatic to be modulated by mindfulness. Alternative explanations are also discussed.

articles.title: Parenting Beyond the Gender Binary: A Scoping Review to Better Conceptualize Gender-Neutral Parenting
articles.authors: Joyce Endendijk; Miriam Holzer; Emma Spruit
articles.abstract: Objective: Recently, there has been an increasing societal and scientific interest in gender-neutral parenting as a means of challenging societal gender norms and achieving equal treatment of people regardless of their gender. Yet, the scientific literature on gender-neutral parenting is fragmented, using different terms and definitions. The present scoping review aimed to clarify how gender-neutral parenting is defined and conceptualized across childhood and adolescence. Design: Following PRISMA guidelines for scoping reviews, a systematic search of the literature published until September 2025 was conducted across different search engines (e.g., Web of Science, Scopus, PsycInfo). In total, 34 publications met predefined eligibility criteria. The content of the publications was analyzed using a hybrid deductive–inductive thematic analysis in NVivo. Results: Across publications, we identified 9 parenting dimensions that clustered within four interrelated systems of action: (a) counter-stereotypical role modelling and reinforcement; (b) disrupting, expanding, and de-centering gender schemas; (c) supporting children’s gender agency and self-determination; and (d) reshaping gendered systems beyond the family context. Together, they form a coherent constellation of parenting practices that we conceptualize as gender-expansive parenting, a term that provides a better fit to the different dimensions than the term gender-neutral parenting. Conclusion: By offering a clear conceptualization and theoretical integration of gender-expansive parenting, this review lays the groundwork for the development of assessment tools and empirical research on how gender-expansive parenting practices shape children’s gender development and well-being.

articles.title: Limited flexibility in Bayesian prior updating for temporal Interval reproduction
articles.authors: Lucy Anne McKeown; Neil Roach
articles.abstract: Bayesian accounts of time perception propose that temporal estimates arise from integrating noisy sensory evidence with prior knowledge about interval statistics. However, the extent to which observers adapt their assumptions about temporal continuity to the structure of the environment remains unclear. We tested whether people flexibly adjust these assumptions during interval reproduction. Across two experiments, participants reproduced intervals drawn either from a randomised sequence or from an autocorrelated random-walk sequence. We also manipulated object context to bias perception toward a single persisting object versus multiple discrete objects, reasoning that temporal continuity may be more likely to be inferred when successive intervals are associated with a common source. Behaviour was evaluated using Bayesian model comparison among a stationary distribution-learning model, a non-stationary tracking model, and a two-state hybrid model capturing intermediate assumptions about temporal continuity. Participants exhibited robust central tendency biases across conditions. However, model fits and Akaike weights provided little evidence that observers adopted stronger assumptions of temporal continuity when intervals were autocorrelated or when object context favoured single-object tracking. Instead, responses were best explained by learning under an effectively stationary prior, with two-state fits indicating only limited contributions of temporal continuity. These findings indicate limited flexibility in prior updating for temporal perception: rather than adapting their assumptions to local temporal structure, observers appear to rely primarily on stable estimates of interval statistics within the session.

articles.title: From the individual to the collective: Complexity in embodied cognitive science
articles.authors: Travis J. Wiltshire
articles.abstract: Embodied cognition, from my view, is the study of, and recognition that, cognition (e.g., mental, perceptual, and action processes) is situated within, and constitutes, a complex dynamical system. This system is multi-scale meaning that understanding aspects of cognition can stem from multiple scales of analysis as small as hormonal levels, to organs, and physiological systems and even to larger collective scales that span individuals (such as couples, teams, and organizations). Importantly, complex systems are fundamentally driven by the interactions of their components and can exhibit both upward and downward causality. While cognitive (neuro) science has often focused on how patterns of brain activity are fundamental and can differentiate between various social/cognitive/emotional states, an embodied cognitive science entails a focus on the dynamical similitude exhibited by complex systems (i.e., how components of different types of systems can exhibit similar dynamics) without primacy of a particular scale of analysis. For example, many types of complex systems exhibit coordination of their components, and both intra- and interpersonal coordination dynamics are drivers of individual and collective cognitive processes. It is from this perspective that I will address the proposed questions and discuss the complexities of embodied cognition from the individual to the collective.

articles.title: Testing the dependency of metacognitive monitoring and executive functions in children: A cross-sectional and longitudinal study.
articles.authors: Donna Bryce; Janina Eberhart
articles.abstract: Accurate metacognitive monitoring is crucial for effective regulation of learning and performance, yet little is known about its cognitive determinants in childhood. The present study investigated the role of executive functions – specifically inhibition and updating of working memory – in children’s metacognitive monitoring accuracy. While prior research has established correlational links between executive functions and metacognitive skills, the current experimental study aimed to provide insight into the causal nature of these relationships by systematically manipulating executive function demands within a task and examining the impact on local monitoring judgment accuracy. Sixty children from two age groups (7 and 9 years) participated, providing cross-sectional data; children in the younger cohort were reassessed approximately 17 months later, contributing longitudinal data. Data were analysed using linear mixed effect models and the results indicated that executive functions and metacognitive monitoring have a dependent relationship in childhood. Moreover, this dependency strengthened with age for inhibition and with repeated task exposure for both inhibition and working memory. These findings are consistent with a competition for resources account of the association between executive functions and metacognitive monitoring, suggesting that when cognitive resources are occupied resolving cognitive conflict or maintaining items in memory, fewer resources remain for monitoring processes and monitoring accuracy suffers. Results are also interpreted within the cue-utilization view of metacognitive monitoring, suggesting developmental changes in the cues children rely on when forming monitoring judgments and a differential dependency of these cues on executive functions.

articles.title: Shared and Diverse Visual Impressions of Portrait Paintings: Agreement, Individual Differences, and Exploratory Directional Structure
articles.authors: Takanori Sano; Hideaki Kawabata
articles.abstract: Portrait paintings provide a useful case study for vision research because they simultaneously evoke judgments of the depicted person’s attractiveness and the painting’s beauty. We examined whether shared visual information and individual aesthetic orientations jointly shape impressions of portrait paintings. In a web-based experiment, 621 Japanese adults rated 100 portraits (50 male and 50 female) on attractiveness of the depicted person, beauty of the painting, abstract–figurative appearance, emotional arousal, and masculinity–femininity. We quantified inter-rater agreement with Mean Minus One (MM1), and explored candidate directed dependencies among impressions and individual differences with the linear non-Gaussian acyclic model (LiNGAM). Beauty showed higher agreement than attractiveness, whereas emotional arousal showed the lowest agreement, supporting a distinction between shared pictorial criteria and viewer-dependent affective responses. Attractiveness and beauty were strongly correlated but differed in the exploratory directional structure. In male portraits, attractiveness emerged as a candidate predictor of beauty; in female portraits, beauty and emotional arousal emerged as candidate predictors of attractiveness. Individual aesthetic traits were linked to final evaluations through masculinity–femininity and emotional arousal. These results suggest that portrait perception combines shared visual constraints with individual aesthetic filters and that portrait sex modulates the balance between face-based, pictorial, and affective processing.

articles.title: Maladaptive Music Listening: A Systematic Review, Thematic Analyses, And Meta-analysis
articles.authors: Kyra Bonus; Maya Breanne Flannery; Lauren K Fink
articles.abstract: Music is a powerful tool for well-being; however, recent research suggests some music-listening behaviours can be maladaptive. Maladaptive music listening (MML) is proposed to be harmful to those engaging in it, but the literature is inconsistent with respect to how MML is defined and measured. We conducted two studies to clarify these issues. Study 1 comprised a systematic PRISMA literature review, with two thematic analyses on definitions and measures of MML. We searched JSTOR, PsycINFO, Web of Science, and ProQuest for original peer-reviewed articles published after 2000; eighteen articles were included in the final analysis. Our thematic analysis on MML definitions identified one major theme, "poor psychological health,” which contained sub-themes “adolescence/youth,” “externalizing problems,” “internalizing problems,” and “inefficient coping.” Measures of MML commonly assessed “interactions with music,” “music preferences,” and “engagement strategies.” Given the association between personality traits and some of the identified themes, Study 2 aimed to meta-analyze their relationship. The original search was conducted with additional terms related to Big Five personality traits. Four articles, comprising 2,225 participants, were included in the final analysis, which examined the relationship between neuroticism and MML, given a lack of articles examining other personality traits. We found a significant moderate pooled effect size between neuroticism and MML (Fisher's Z value of 0.21 [0.16–0.25]) and no evidence of publication bias. Overall, this work clarifies the existing definitions, measures, and findings on MML to guide future research, increase construct validity, and help predict or prevent MML in vulnerable individuals.

articles.title: From Neural Decoding to Neural Symbols: co-creating meaning from brain activity
articles.authors: Makoto Fukushima; Tim Puphal; Yukiko Kikuchi; Shinsuke Suzuki
articles.abstract: Human behavior externalizes only a fraction of what the brain processes.　Here we argue for the potential of Neural Symbolic Communication: rendering neural activity as shared sensory objects whose meaning is co-created rather than decoded, opening a complementary channel for human-human and human-AI collaboration.

articles.title: The genetic landscape of brain ageing
articles.authors: Phoebe Imms; Briar Wormington; Tania Islam; Damian J Woodward; Christelle Doppenberg; Shang-Heng Tsai; Nicholas J Kim; Andrei Irimia; Eske M Derks
articles.abstract: Brain age gap (BAG) has emerged as a widely used measure of brain health, with applications in neuropsychiatric prognostication and clinical trial enrichment. Over the past eight years, 23 genome‑wide association studies (GWAS) in more than 62,000 adults have advanced the current understanding of genetic contributions to brain ageing. BAG is moderately heritable, with common variants explaining up to 29% of phenotypic variance in the population. This systematic review and re-analysis consolidates current knowledge of the genetic architecture of brain ageing and highlights the divergence in identified variants across brain age estimation methodologies. Across studies, 195 genes have been associated with brain age, with seven (PLEKHM1, MAPT, KANSL1, CRHR1, SPPL2C, ARHGAP27, and STH) consistently identified. These converge on pathways related to neurodevelopment, cytoskeletal stability, stress responsivity, and cellular maintenance. Differences in BAG modelling produce distinct genetic profiles: shallow‑learning and multimodal approaches tend to implicate genes linked to neurodegeneration (e.g., APOE), whereas deep learning of T1-weighted images more often highlights microstructural and intracellular signalling pathways. Functional annotation further suggests that BAG reflects broadly distributed biological processes rather than brain‑exclusive mechanisms, instead capturing aspects of systemic integrity that are relevant to central nervous system function. Accordingly, BAG may be best understood not as a disease‑specific biomarker, but as a quantitative endophenotype reflecting cumulative deviation from normative brain integrity.

articles.title: Children need structural explanations for social inequalities, and educators who can provide them
articles.authors: Rebecca Peretz-Lange
articles.abstract: Children are highly aware of social inequalities by the preschool years, and they spontaneously generate explanations to make sense of them. In particular, children tend to intuitively attribute social inequalities to intrinsic differences (e.g., differences in groups’ inborn abilities) rather than extrinsic differences (e.g., differences in groups’ circumstances) – that is, they intuitively engage in essentialist reasoning rather than structural reasoning. Essentialist reasoning is associated with a host of pernicious outcomes for children’s friendship preferences, academic motivation, and more. One promising approach for undermining children’s essentialist assumptions is to point out the extrinsic causes of social inequalities to children. Of course, in order for teachers to do so, they must have knowledge of these extrinsic causes themselves, which requires significant expertise. A growing body of work finds that education (in disciplines ranging from history to biology) fosters a more structural understanding of social inequalities, which teachers can then transmit to children, either explicitly or implicitly. Thus, children deserve highly-educated teachers whose training includes not only crucial teaching- and content-related knowledge, but also the broad liberal arts foundation that fosters a structural worldview. This article reviews the scientific literature on children’s explanations for social inequalities and highlights its implications for teacher training.

articles.title: The development and initial validation of the Perinatal Intrusions Interpretation Index: a novel scale that measures negative appraisals of infant-related intrusive thoughts
articles.authors: Jodie Ellen Pestana; Yan Lin; Nichole Fairbrother; Ariane Beeston; Yasmin Hasan; Florencia Canessa; Sarah Daniels; Emily Morgan; Nita-Roya Roschanzamir; Lucy Zhang
articles.abstract: Objectives: Unwanted and often distressing intrusive thoughts of infant-related harm are common during the perinatal period and are associated with poorer maternal mental health. The mechanisms linking perinatal intrusive thoughts to mental health remain poorly understood. One proposed avenue is through maladaptive appraisals, yet there currently are no measures capturing perinatal-specific appraisals. The aim of the current study was to develop and validate a novel Perinatal Intrusions Interpretation Index (PIII) to assess negative appraisals related to intrusions of infant-related harm. Methods: 439 people who were 1–6 months postpartum completed 12 items capturing appraisals and an adapted online version of the Postpartum Intrusions Interview. A second validation sample, N = 142 people ≤ 9 months postpartum, completed the final 10-item PIII. Results: Exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses indicated a three-factor structure of the PIII: 1) inflated responsibility, 2) importance of thoughts, and 3) need for control. The total PIII and subscales demonstrated good internal consistency. Higher negative appraisals on the PIII were significantly associated with more frequent and distressing accidental and intentional infant-related harm intrusive thoughts and maladaptive behavioural responses. Intrusion type (accidental versus intentional) moderated the relationship between negative appraisals and intrusion frequency and distress, and frequency of behavioural responses. Conclusions: The PIII is a reliable and valid scale to assess negative appraisals of infant-related harm intrusions. Negative appraisals may be a cognitive risk factor for perinatal intrusions to progress from normative to functionally impairing, offering a modifiable target for the prevention and treatment of perinatal anxiety disorders.

articles.title: Selective Attention Can Bias Prosocial Learning From Consequences
articles.authors: Glen William Spiteri; Zeyiting Gao; Seamus Kim; Yina Sun; Falk Lieder
articles.abstract: People make many decisions in which increasing the benefits for some people reduces the benefits for others. What determines which lessons people learn from the outcomes of those decisions? We propose that selective attention can bias what people learn from such decisions. We tested this hypothesis across four preregistered experiments and an internal meta-analysis pooling data from 11,603 participants. In each experiment, participants made decisions in a social dilemma pitting the interests of a financially stable ingroup against those of a distant, impoverished outgroup. Critically, when participants subsequently learned about the consequences of their previous decision, an experimental manipulation selectively directed their attention to its effect on their ingroup, its effect on the outgroup, or irrelevant information. Across all experiments, directing attention to outgroup consequences in the previous decision increased subsequent donations to the outgroup, while directing attention to the previous decision’s ingroup consequences reinforced parochialism. These effects accumulated over repeated decisions, with learning trajectories diverging as a function of attention condition. The meta-analysis pointed toward meaningful prosocial learning effects of both outgroup-directed attention (d = 0.36 vs. control) and ingroup-directed attention (d=−0.21 vs. control), with a medium-sized intergroup contrast (d= 0.56). Empathic concern for the victim of a past decision partially mediated the effect of directing attention to consequences for the ingroup versus the outgroup. These findings demonstrate that prosocial learning is shaped by which consequences people attend to.

articles.title: The Linguistic Correlates of Symptom Severity in Depression: An Observational Study in Web-Based Forum Users
articles.authors: David Owen; Antonio F Pardiñas; Jose Camacho Collados
articles.abstract: Depression is a psychiatric disorder that is highly prevalent worldwide, yet people often do not consult a clinician during its onset. They may instead convey their experience on social media platforms or in web-based forums. The development of automatic methods for detecting depression in these online spaces is growing. However, methods for gauging the severity of depression and the severity of different depression symptoms are less well explored. Such methods may improve our ability to detect severe depression early in users of these online spaces. In this study, we used datasets that contain the posts of Reddit users. Each user provided a completed BDI-II questionnaire, which revealed the severity of their depression and the severity of different depression symptoms. We extracted linguistic features from the users' posts, including first-person singular pronouns, negative emotion words, and absolutist words. We then performed regression analyses to understand the relationships between these linguistic features and the severity of depression and its symptoms. Our findings showed significant associations with the overall severity of depression, particularly with regard to negative emotion words. These results may have uses to improve methods for detecting early signs of depression and gauge its severity in the absence of formal tests. Our analysis did not find any associations between language features and fine-grained metrics of severity for individual depression symptoms. As these associations are not implausible, larger datasets may be needed to improve our linguistic understanding of different symptoms and symptom domains.

articles.title: Pediatric Cognitive Functioning Before, During, and After the COVID-19 Pandemic: Domain Specificity and School-Context Differences in a Large Multisite Sample
articles.authors: Tyler Maxwell Moore; Ruben C. Gur; Kosha Ruparel; J. Cobb Scott; Nancy Weinstein; Nancy Tsai
articles.abstract:
Background: The COVID-19 pandemic disrupted children's educational and developmental environments, but its consequences have been studied mainly through academic achievement. We examined whether objective neurocognitive performance differed before, during, and after the pandemic, and whether differences were domain-, context-, and metric-specific rather than global.
Method: Participants were 33,459 children and adolescents (M age = 13.93 years, SD = 2.49; 48.4% female) assessed January 2018-December 2024 with the Penn Computerized Neurocognitive Battery. COVID period was coded as pre-pandemic (n = 4,411), acute disruption (n = 5,208), and post-acute (n = 23,840). Age-standardized accuracy, speed, and efficiency scores across nine domains were analyzed with linear mixed-effects models (children nested within families), with school type as a focal factor, and income group and sex as covariates.
Results: Period-related differences were robust but domain- and metric-specific. Verbal and spatial memory were lower during and after the pandemic, with spatial memory showing the largest effect; spatial memory speed continued to slow post-acutely. Response speed slowed across several domains, often without loss of accuracy and sometimes with improved accuracy (e.g., abstract reasoning). Attention, by contrast, was faster during and after the pandemic and more efficient afterward, with progressive improvement in efficiency and speed. The COVID Period × School Type interaction was nonsignificant, though the consistency of the dominant patterns across school types was visually uneven.
Conclusions: Pandemic-period cognitive functioning reflected changes within specific cognitive systems rather than uniform decline. Memory was most vulnerable and several effects persisted post-acutely, whereas attention and reasoning accuracy were preserved or enhanced. Separating efficiency, accuracy, and speed is essential, and speed effects warrant replication.
Keywords: neurocognition, COVID-19, pandemic, lockdown, virtual learning

articles.title: An MDS-REM Model for Predicting Individual-Item Perceptual Old-New Recognition
articles.authors: Robert Nosofsky; Adam F Osth
articles.abstract: The Retrieving Effectively for Memory (REM) model (Shiffrin & Stevyers, 1997) is an extremely influential model of old-new recognition memory based on Bayesian reasoning principles that provides a comprehensive account of diverse memory phenomena.  However, a limitation of extant versions of the model is that it does not provide accounts of recognition memory at the level of individual items based on their precise positions in multidimensional similarity space and their possession of item-specific distinctive features.  Instead, it assumes a geometric probability distribution for generating hypothetical features and relies on computer simulation to generate predictions of patterns of results for large classes of items and experimental manipulations.  Here we move in the direction of filling that gap by proposing a REM-like model in which individual items are represented in one-to-one correspondence as points in multidimensional similarity (MDS) spaces and in which information regarding distinctive features possessed by individual objects is also provided.  Rather than using the geometric-probability distribution envisioned by Shiffrin and Steyvers, this “MDS-REM” model uses continuous probability density functions defined over the continuous-dimension MDS spaces.
