articles.authors: Mikaela Richardson; Rahul Ashwin Masurkar; Lilyan Tyson; Adam Vasarhelyi; Kalia White; Khalisa Amir Hamzah; Gia Nhi Lam; Sarah Olsson; Ottmar V. Lipp; Casey Agassiz
articles.abstract: Fear conditioning is most commonly assessed by measuring electrodermal activity to a conditioned stimulus (CS) in anticipation of an electric shock or another unconditioned stimulus (US). Replacing the electric shock with aversive film clips is a recent innovation that potentially has higher ecological validity for posttraumatic stress disorder. The present report examined boundary conditions of this new paradigm across two experiments, with a particular focus on the effectiveness of film clip versus electric shock USs in promoting physiological fear conditioning. In Experiment 1, we tested whether fear acquisition was influenced by the inclusion of a shock US, prior exposure to a longer trauma film, or the use of face versus shape conditioned stimuli (CSs). Fear acquisition was enhanced by the inclusion of a shock US and to a lesser extent by prior trauma film exposure; however, conditioning in groups using film clip USs alone was characterised by lack of conditioned electrodermal responding. Experiment 2 investigated whether this absence of conditioned responding reflected reduced contingency awareness by measuring online US expectancy across film-based and shock-based US conditions. Despite equivalent US expectancy, CS pleasantness, and subjective US ratings across groups, conditioned electrodermal responses during acquisition were observed only in the shock US condition. Differences between groups may be explained by differences in salivary cortisol reactivity, with higher cortisol responses following acquisition in the shock group. Together, these findings indicate that shock USs increase physiological arousal, which appears to be essential for electrodermal reactivity, irrespective of conditioned learning processes. This finding has potentially important implications for the interpretation of electrodermal measurement in fear conditioning paradigms.

articles.title: DBT Skills Video Intervention for Chinese/Chinese American College Students: A Randomized Controlled Trial
articles.authors: Qingqing Yin; Shireen L. Rizvi
articles.abstract: Psychotherapy delivered in its traditional format is unlikely to benefit Asian Americans (AA) due to low rates of treatment utilization and retention. Brief videos teaching Dialectical Behavior Therapy (DBT) skills provides an alternative avenue to disseminate emotion regulation resources. The integration of behavioral change strategies and Zen Buddhist philosophies (e.g., acceptance) in DBT may also be culturally appealing to some AA subgroups. In this study, we evaluated the acceptability/usability and outcomes of a video-based DBT skills intervention among a sample of Chinese/Chinese American individuals. The intervention was comprised of 14 brief animated videos of DBT skills. A total of 91 Chinese/Chinese American college students, not currently receiving treatment, completed daily assessment for four weeks and were randomized to receive (1) assessment-only (n = 29), (2) acceptance-oriented followed by change-oriented skills videos (n = 32), or (3) change-oriented followed by acceptance-oriented skills videos (n = 30). Self-reports and engagement behaviors supported the acceptability/usability of the intervention, which was not found to differ between change- or acceptance-oriented skills videos. Compared to the control group, the intervention groups showed more favorable outcomes related to the distress and management of emotional experiences. This study provides insights of acceptable and effective ways to address mental health needs of Asian/Asian Americans while extending the scarce literature on this topic.

articles.title: Comments on Réale, Dall, and Dingemanse (2026). Praise, and a pathway for integrating the study of personality evolution
articles.authors: Alexander Weiss
articles.abstract: Réale, Dall, and Dingemanse have contributed a valuable commentary, both in terms of clarifying how to (and not to) consider “personality traits” and in, perhaps unknowingly, providing a glimmer of a bridge that can unify the study of animal and human personality. My comments reveal the bridge in all its glory.

articles.title: A SOCIAL IDENTITY MODEL OF LEADERSHIP DEVELOPMENT IMPLEMENTATION
articles.authors: Blake McMillan; S. Alexander Haslam; Tyree Mitchell; Niklas K Steffens; Kim Olivia Peters
articles.abstract:
Despite substantial investment in leadership development, organizations often struggle to
implement relevant programs effectively. This reflects the fact that the success of program
implementation is contingent on identity dynamics. Building on the Social Identity Model of
Leadership, the ASPIRe model, and evidence-based programs such as 5R that apply these
principles, we argue that, to be effective, implementation needs to ensure that the approach
makes sense for “us”, aligns with who “we” are, and fits with “our” leadership. To guide this
process, we present a Social Identity Model of Leadership Development Implementation
(SIMoLDI) which specifies four phases of effective implementation: (1) identity activation, (2)
identity alignment, (3) identity actualization, and (4) identity anchoring. Each phase draws on
distinct identity leadership components: prototypicality, entrepreneurship, advancement, and
impresarioship. The principles we outline have general relevance in providing a practical, theory-
informed framework for translating leadership development initiatives into sustainable practice,
while being particularly applicable when leadership development is focused on building
collective capability.

articles.title: Prototype principle explains aesthetics for general visual experiences beyond isolated objects
articles.authors: Yi-Chia Chen; Shuhao Fu; Derek Feng; Moriah Taylor; Jeff Chang; Xiaoyang Chi; Hongjing Lu
articles.abstract: A salient aspect of our daily visual experiences is the aesthetic impressions. Why do we enjoy some views but not others? Researchers have found visual attributes that we enjoy seeing for colors, shapes, and objects, and even for human faces and bodies; however, aesthetic preferences for holistic visual experiences—views that encompass many different objects and attributes—remain largely undescribed. What principles govern holistic visual aesthetics beyond preferences for certain objects or features? We found computational evidence in support of the prototype principle for visual aesthetics. We measure each view’s prototypicality based on its average similarity to a large reference set of images in feature spaces from pretrained deep convolutional neural networks (AlexNet and VGG-16). For views consisting of inanimate content, the more prototypical the high-level visual representations are, the more aesthetically pleasing the views appear. This prototype effect suggests a functional answer to why we like what we like: We like typical visual experiences that are common, safe, or neutral. Thus, aesthetic preferences from holistic visual experiences are systematic, explainable, and reflect the underlying organization of visual representations of the world. Our method demonstrates a new way to explore both vision and aesthetics using computational models—besides investigating specific visual properties or isolated objects, we can also explore the organization of visual representations and aesthetic experiences holistically, getting us one step closer to understanding how we see, what we like, and why we like what we like in everyday life.

articles.title: Geographically Segregated Culture is associated with Lower Mobility, Weaker Democracy, and Risk of Civil Conflict
articles.authors: Cindel J. M. White; Michael Muthukrishna
articles.abstract: Stable nations require strangers to coordinate and cooperate despite cultural differences. Using the Cultural Fixation Index (CFST) on World Values Survey data (more than 260,000 participants; 95 countries; 2005–2022), we quantified within-country cultural distances between regions, ethnicities, religious groups, education levels, and social classes, to predict various measures of social mobility, democracy, and civil conflict. A pre-registered multiverse analysis (54,600 model specifications; 100 model families; 6 demographic groupings; 6 outcome measures) showed only one robust pattern of negative societal outcomes: larger cultural distance between geographic regions is associated with higher corruption, weaker democracy, lower social mobility, and greater risk of civil conflict. Distances between ethnic, religious, and socioeconomic groups were mostly benign, and educational distance was often associated with better outcomes. The results imply that what matters is not diversity per se, but whether culturally distinct groups are geographically segregated and therefore less likely to regularly interact to negotiate the cultural traits needed for cooperation and coordination.

articles.title: Relationship between sensory processing sensitivity and rejection sensitivity and their association with mental health
articles.authors: Jacob I. Stephens; Lindsey B. Hinkle; Zoe A. Childers-Rockey; Charlie Rioux
articles.abstract: Sensory processing sensitivity (SPS) and rejection sensitivity (RS) are two distinct sensitivity-related traits that have each been associated with poorer mental health. However, little research has examined how these constructs relate to one another or whether they uniquely contribute to mental health. This study examined the association between SPS and RS and their independent relationships with mental distress and well-being in an online sample of 565 adults. Participants self-reported SPS, RS, psychological distress, and well-being. Correlations and multiple linear regressions were conducted to examine associations between SPS, RS, distress, and well-being, both before and after adjusting for sociodemographic characteristics. While both traits independently predicted psychological distress, RS demonstrated a stronger and more robust association with psychological well-being after accounting for sociodemographic factors. These findings suggest that assessing both SPS and RS may improve understanding of individual differences in mental health and inform more targeted prevention and intervention strategies.

articles.title: A rapid assessment of pragmatic abilities and cognitive substrates: The German APACS Brief
articles.authors: Lena Sophie Wilkens; Laura Anna Ciaccio; Thomas Picht; Marta Bosia; Giorgio Arcara; Valentina Bambini; Rosario Tomasello
articles.abstract:
Background
Clinical evaluation of language abilities is central to diagnosing impairments in neurological and neuropsychiatric conditions, such as brain injuries, Parkinson’s disease, or schizophrenia. However, assessment tools predominantly target formal structural aspects of language, including phonological, lexical-semantic, and syntactic processing, while pragmatic and communicative abilities remain underrepresented, despite consistent evidence of their vulnerability across clinical populations. This gap is largely due to the scarcity of standardized and rapid tools for pragmatic assessment and the inherent difficulty of measuring context-dependent communicative abilities.
Aim
This study aimed to develop and validate the German adaptation of the Assessment of Pragmatic Abilities and Cognitive Substrates Brief (APACS Brief-De), a 10-minute screening tool originally created in Italian, assessing discourse production and comprehension of figurative language (metaphor and humor) in German-speaking contexts, to evaluate the psychometric properties, usability, and cross-linguistic applicability of the instrument.
Methods
Adopting a culturally sensitive translation approach, a standard and a multiple-choice APACS Brief-De were developed, each with an alternate form to allow for repeated assessments, which were administered remotely to healthy German-speaking adults.
Results
The APACS Brief-De Multiple Choice showed good consistency, reliability, validity, and equivalence between forms. Increasing age and lower global cognitive functioning were significantly associated with reduced pragmatic performance.  The comparisons with the Italian standard form confirmed statistical equivalence, underscoring the robustness of the tool across languages. Age- and education-adjusted normative cut-off scores are provided for clinical interpretation.
Conclusions
APACS Brief-De offers a rapid and valid tool for assessing global pragmatic abilities, well suited for integration into routine clinical practice, and represents a significant step toward crosslinguistic standardization of pragmatic assessment.

articles.title: Reduced speech-to-song transformation for native-language speech in Mandarin Chinese listeners
articles.authors: Makiko Sadakata; Yuzhu Gu
articles.abstract: Why does a listener's linguistic background shape whether repeated speech comes to sound like music? Previous studies have reported that speakers of tonal languages experience a weaker Speech-to-Song (STS) transformation, in which repeated speech comes to sound increasingly musical. It remains unclear, however, whether this reduction reflects a general property of tonal-language listeners or arises specifically when they hear their native language. We compared native Mandarin Chinese, English, and Dutch listeners' responses to English speech, Mandarin Chinese speech, and non-speech stimuli (data collected 2024– 2026) before and after repeated presentation. All groups reliably experienced the STS transformation. Critically, however, the transformation was markedly reduced only when native Mandarin Chinese listeners heard Mandarin Chinese speech. The same listeners showed a typical transformation for English speech, and English and Dutch listeners showed comparable transformations for both languages. Furthermore, this reduction disappeared when linguistic information was removed while preserving the original pitch contours. These findings indicate that reduced transformation is not a general characteristic of tonal-language listeners but depends on whether pitch remains available for lexical interpretation. The results suggest that the linguistic function of pitch constrains its reinterpretation as melody, a pattern consistent with predictive-coding accounts of speech and music perception.

articles.title: The Mind's Eye of the Adopter: Visual Stereotypes of Dogs and Cats
articles.authors: Lindsay Palmer; Daniel N Albohn; Alexander Todorov; Anamarie C. Johnson; Reginald B. Adams; Joseph C. Brandenburg; Clive DL Wynne
articles.abstract: The influence of visual appearance on pet adoption is poorly understood, partially due to inconsistent findings. We examined visual biases in the appearance of dogs and cats using a novel data-driven method that leverages generative AI to visualize mental prototypes at both the individual and group levels. The results demonstrated both strong idiosyncratic preferences and shared, group-level consistencies, offering an explanation for previously reported inconsistencies. Importantly, we found that greater similarity between images of real shelter animals and the group prototypes of “adoptable” dogs and cats, as well as “friendly” dogs, was associated with a shorter time in the shelter before adoption. This study provides novel evidence for the interplay between idiosyncratic variation and shared biases in shaping visual stereotypes of companion animals.

articles.title: Beyond the Label: Capturing Nuanced Head Nod Distinctions in ASL and TİD via Pose Estimation and DTW
articles.authors: Serpil Karabüklü; Emre Hakguder; Diane Brentari
articles.abstract: Sign language research has long recognized that head nods participate in a wide range of linguistic functions, including prosody, semantics, and discourse. However, these movements are typically described using categorical labels (e.g., head nod), obscuring how continuous movement maps onto linguistic function and making it difficult to determine whether different functions recruit the same articulatory gesture or distinct kinematic realizations. This study investigates whether head nods associated with different linguistic functions differ in their internal movement organization and whether these distinctions are shared across sign languages. We analyzed 608 head nods produced by 19 Deaf signers of American Sign Language (ASL) and Turkish Sign Language (TİD). Head movement trajectories were extracted using computer vision-based keypoint estimation and examined through complementary analyses of kinematic features and Dynamic Time Warping (DTW). Results revealed three main findings. First, semantic and prosodic head nods systematically differed in their kinematic organization: semantic head nods exhibited greater peak prominence, whereas prosodic head nods exhibited greater trough prominence in both languages. Second, these form-function mappings were shared across ASL and TİD, suggesting common principles linking kinematic structure to linguistic function. Third, trajectory-based analyses revealed language-specific differences that were not captured by individual kinematic features: prosodic head nods showed distinct trajectories across languages, whereas semantic head nods remained highly similar. These findings demonstrate that linguistic distinctions are encoded not only in individual movement features but also in the temporal organization of continuous movement. More broadly, the findings suggest that linguistic information in sign languages is organized not only across articulatory channels but also within the temporal organization of movement. Rather than the gesture label itself, specific kinematic realizations constitute the relevant units linking continuous movement to linguistic function.

articles.title: Assessing Fairness in AI-Assisted Writing Scoring: Two Indices for Quantifying the Magnitude of Group Differences
articles.authors: Guanyu Chen; Sirui Wu; Chiyu Zhang; Amery D. Wu
articles.abstract: Fairness evaluation in automated essay scoring (AES) requires more than determining whether group differences exist. It also requires evidence about how large those differences are, which group they favor, and whether they warrant further attention. This study introduces two model-level indices, Conditional Mean Disparity (CMD) and Conditional Odds Disparity (COD), for evaluating group differences in predicted writing scores after accounting for human-rated proficiency. CMD quantifies disparity on the predicted score scale, whereas COD quantifies disparity using the relative odds of receiving higher predicted scores. The indices were demonstrated using writing samples from the PERSUADE 2.0 corpus and four AES systems representing traditional statistical modeling, deep learning, and prompt-based large language model scoring. The findings showed that CMD and COD provided interpretable estimates of disparity magnitude across systems and captured information that was not reflected in scoring performance alone. By emphasizing the size and direction of observed group differences, the proposed indices can support fairness evaluation, model comparison, and decisions about whether further examination is needed.

articles.title: A Behavioural Investigation of Multisensory Integration in Youth with Attention-Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder
articles.authors: Carolynn Hare; Bernice Leung; Glenda Zhai; YuHe Li; Ryan A Stevenson
articles.abstract: Multisensory integration is a key sensory process which has a role in cognitive development. Multisensory integration has been demonstrated to be affected in ADHD largely in adults, but findings have been inconsistent. In this study, we examined whether multisensory integration differed in youth (ages 4-17) with ADHD (n=53) and without ADHD (n=60) using three different behavioural tasks (i.e., SIFI, McGurk, and speech-in-noise). No group differences were found in the SIFI, but ADHD youth showed reduced susceptibility to the McGurk illusion compared to neurotypical (NT) youth. The speech-in-noise task revealed no differences in multisensory gain, though hyperactive-impulsive traits were trending negatively related to phoneme accuracy. Overall, the results suggest reduced multisensory integration in youth with ADHD, using tasks involving speech stimuli. These results suggest that stimulus complexity may be important to examine for multisensory integration in ADHD, and further, multisensory integration may be affected across development in ADHD.

articles.title: Child Multilingualisms Beyond WEIRD Contexts: Evidence from Asia and Africa
articles.authors: Alexandra Paquette; Leher Singh
articles.abstract: Who is the language learner represented in language acquisition research? Despite the prevalence and diversity of multilingual childhoods, theories of early language development remain grounded in monolinguals from Euro-American contexts, while multilingual research has concentrated on limited populations/settings. This review examines multilingual language development during the first three years across Asia and Africa, attending to diversity within and between regions. Research on input, speech perception, word recognition, and vocabulary indicate that multilingual infants flexibly adapt to linguistic ecologies, but vary in developmental pathways. We argue that multilingualism should be conceptualized not as a categorical characteristic, but as a multidimensional ecology structured by language combinations, caregiving arrangements, social functions, socioeconomic conditions, and colonial histories. We conclude with a research agenda that broadens empirical and linguistic coverage, improves measurement of multilingual experiences, and centers community-informed priorities. A globally adequate science of language development requires building theory from children’s diverse multilingual realities.

articles.title: For Whom Do School-Based Mindfulness Programs Work? The Role of Personality in Adolescent Intervention Outcomes
articles.authors: Maria Anna Wasylkowska; Dorota Kobylinska; Julian Mituniewicz; Szymon Szumiał; Pawel Holas
articles.abstract:
Abstract
Objectives
School-based mindfulness programs (SBMPs) are increasingly implemented to support adolescent mental health, yet evidence for their effectiveness remains mixed. Recent research suggests that average effects may obscure meaningful variability in outcomes across individuals. The present study aimed to examine both the overall effectiveness of a 6-week SBMP and the role of personality traits in predicting individual differences in intervention outcomes. 
Method
This quasi-experimental study included 122 adolescents aged 12–14 years from 14 school classes, assigned to either an intervention group or a wait-list control group. Outcomes were assessed at pre-intervention, post-intervention, and 3-month follow-up, including anxiety, emotion regulation difficulties, well-being, mindfulness, psychological distress, and self-compassion. Personality traits (neuroticism, extraversion, and openness) were examined as predictors of differential response to the intervention using latent class growth analysis and logistic regression. 
Results 
At the group level, the SBMP did not produce significant effects across the examined outcomes compared to the control condition. However, person-centered analyses revealed meaningful heterogeneity in response patterns. Adolescents characterized by higher neuroticism and lower extraversion were more likely to show improvements across multiple domains, including reduced anxiety and psychological distress and increased well-being and mindfulness. Additionally, lower openness predicted improvement in psychological distress. These findings suggest that intervention effects were not uniform but concentrated among adolescents with greater baseline vulnerability.
Conclusions 
These results indicate that the effectiveness of SBMPs may depend less on average effects and more on individual differences in responsiveness. Mindfulness training may be particularly beneficial for adolescents with specific personality profiles associated with higher psychological vulnerability. These results highlight the importance of moving beyond universal approaches toward more targeted implementation of mindfulness-based programs in school settings. 
Keywords: mindfulness, adolescence, personality, training, SBMPs

articles.title: Ordinality and dyscalculia: what do we actually know?
articles.authors: Declan Devlin; Natalia Dubinkina; Pirjo Aunio
articles.abstract: Over the past two decades, there has been increasing interest in the role of order processing in developmental dyscalculia. In this review, we consider the literature on how people with dyscalculia process ordinal information and the cognitive and affective factors that contribute to observed deficits. Across studies, children and adults with dyscalculia consistently show impaired performance on a range of order processing tasks, including symbolic numerical order verification, order production, and event ordering tasks. These findings have led some researchers to conclude that dyscalculia is characterised by a general deficit in order processing. However, other evidence suggests these deficits may emerge only for certain sequences, implying more specific underlying mechanisms (e.g., working memory deficits). We argue that these contrasting conclusions largely reflect the relatively coarse level at which order processing has typically been investigated and thus encourage more fine-grained approaches that distinguish between tasks, items, and their underlying cognitive demands.

articles.title: Two Identities, One Alliance? Catalysts and Constraints of Dual Identification for Allyship Formation
articles.authors: Jonas R. Kunst; John Dovidio
articles.abstract: Allyship—actions by advantaged-group members supporting marginalized groups—is shaped by how groups define “us.” Common-ingroup appeals (e.g., “we are all Americans”) broaden goodwill but often obscure power imbalances, stalling action. Dual-identity appeals (e.g., “Black and American”) can mobilize allies by highlighting injustice. Yet, they risk triggering suspicions of divided loyalty when groups feel threatened. Integrating social, cultural, and evolutionary psychology, we map the catalysts that facilitate and the constraints that inhibit dual-identity allyship. This framework emphasizes reciprocal influences between groups and highlights the importance of marginalized-group receptivity to allyship efforts. We translate these processes into an actionable policy matrix based on perceived injustice and intergroup threat. The matrix specifies when to emphasize dual identities for justice, when to prioritize threat reduction to ensure receptivity, or when to sequence both approaches. Clarifying when a dual identity sustains allyship equips practitioners with tools for lasting intergroup cooperation.

articles.title: Ten simple rules for achieving computational reproducibility in cognitive neuroscience
articles.authors: Gaurav Mahajan; Caroline J Charpentier; Valentin Guigon
articles.abstract:
Computational research depends on complex, linked operations. In cognitive neuroscience, these operations often combine multiple data types, specialized toolboxes, custom scripts, and changing computing environments. Open science practices, Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) principles, and data standardization have improved how research objects are shared and described. However, they do not guarantee that the same analysis can be rerun to reconstruct the original result. This limitation becomes more consequential as AI-assisted coding tools are accelerating code development, with the potential to strengthen good practices, but also to amplify weak ones. Related problems have long been addressed in software engineering and machine learning operations through practices that make code, data, environments, and execution steps traceable. Drawing from these practices, we present ten simple rules for achieving computational reproducibility in cognitive neuroscience. We emphasize simple, low-cost decisions that can be implemented early and scaled as
projects become more complex.

articles.title: When Does Cognitive Ability Matter for Vote Choice? Ideological Orientation as a Moderator in the 2024 U.S. Presidential Election
articles.authors: Till Lubczyk; André Kretzschmar
articles.abstract: Cognitive ability predicts vote choice, but does it do so equally across the ideological spectrum? In a preregistered longitudinal study, U.S. young adults (N = 594) completed a broad cognitive ability assessment and five ideology measures (right-wing authoritarianism, social dominance orientation, social and economic conservatism, political self-placement) before the 2024 presidential election and reported their vote afterwards. Lower cognitive ability and stronger right-wing orientations each predicted voting for Trump, replicating prior findings; these associations held when controlling for demographics, including education and household income. Critically, Local Structural Equation Modeling revealed that ideology moderated the cognitive ability-vote choice association: it was robust among liberal and moderate voters but faded to near zero at high levels of right-wing commitment for four of five measures. The findings are consistent with motivated cognition accounts and challenge the assumption that reasoning ability plays a uniform role in electoral decision-making.

articles.title: A dynamic theory of multi-agent goal pursuit in continuous time and space
articles.authors: Anderson K. Fitch; Peter D. Kvam
articles.abstract: Many of the goals that people pursue in everyday life involve dynamic social interactions with others who have their own latent goals. Modeling how these goals manifest in behavior and how different goals interact with one another is central to effectively explaining and predicting the dynamics of human interactions. In this paper, we develop a theory that postulates a balance of global and local objectives driving behavior, combining elements of control theory and approach-avoidance to predict complex movement and dyadic interactions in real time. We apply this model to explain movement in a continuous control task, where participants use a joystick to accomplish a variety of direct (attack / avoid / inspect the other player) and indirect (defend a location from the other player / herd the other player to a location) goals. In the first experiment, participants interacted with a computer opponent. In the second experiment, participants interacted with other participants who had an independent goal. The goal pursuit model successfully accounted for player movement across time as people dynamically adapted to their opponent's behavior, providing insights into participants' trial-specific and person-specific priorities. In addition, the model parameters were used to identify participants' latent goals in both the single-player and two-player tasks, yielding superior performance to classifiers based on raw behavior. Put together, the model can support real-time behavioral prediction and intent inference even in complex multi-agent interactions faced by humans and social AI.

articles.title: Hive Immunity: How the Social Brain Aligns Immune Systems for Collective Protection
articles.authors: Simone Shamay-Tsoory
articles.abstract: Pathogens create a fundamental tension in social life. Although close social bonds enable caregiving and group cohesion, they also increase exposure to infection. To address this tension, extant theories have suggested that sickness behaviors evolved primarily to counteract infection through avoidance and withdrawal as protective responses to illness. However, emerging evidence suggests that illness can also elicit approach toward caregivers. Here, I propose the immune alignment theory, which suggests that immune responses may become coordinated between infected individuals and their close social partners. The theory holds that perceiving sickness in close others, may trigger matched preparatory immune changes in the uninfected observer. This response may facilitate caregiving while enhancing self-protection. In terms of neural correlates, immune alignment is likely mediated by brain–immune and brain-to-brain interactions and supported by neural systems involved in reward, salience, and interbrain synchrony. The immune alignment theory offers a framework for understanding how social relationships shape immune regulation beyond the individual body, with implications for caregiving, psychopathology, and collective health. Direct empirical tests of immune alignment remain an important direction for future research.

articles.title: Visual information selected during active viewing is sufficient to drive similar aesthetic evaluations in passive viewers: Evidence from ‘attentional transplants’
articles.authors: Hong B Nguyen; Benjamin van Buren
articles.abstract: Aesthetically evaluating a scene typically involves active viewing, where one controls what one sees and when. Active viewing includes planning where to look, moving, and selecting information—any of which could influence aesthetic judgments. Using a method of ‘attentional transplants’, we show that information selected during active viewing is sufficient to cause similar aesthetic evaluations even in passive viewers: First, online ‘donors’ actively viewed scenes through a cursor-controlled window and rated their aesthetic pleasingness. Next, new ‘recipients’ passively viewed the scenes through windows replaying the viewing pattern of the donor who liked the scene most, or least. Recipients gave substantially higher ratings to scenes after seeing the selection patterns of donors who most liked (vs. disliked) them. Subsequent experiments found that selection patterns which drive greater liking allow better prediction of upcoming information. Thus, visual information selected during active viewing, independent of active control, is sufficient to drive aesthetic evaluations.

articles.title: Feeling the way to words: Parents' speech and touch cues highlight word-to-world mappings of body parts. Language Learning and Development,
articles.authors: No authors listed
articles.abstract:
Touch cues might facilitate infants’ early word comprehension and explain why body part words
emerge so early. Parents were instructed to teach their infants, 4- to 5-month-olds or 10- to 11-
month-olds, nonce words for body parts and a contrast object but were given no instructions
about the use of touch. Parents spontaneously touched target body parts in close timing to
uttering the target nonce words. They did not show this alignment for unrelated touches and
nonce words. Moreover, when parents used this temporally synchronized speech and touch input,
infants looked more frequently to the target locations on their bodies and to their parent’s faces
compared to when the input was mismatched or only speech. Similar to other research on parents' use of speech and gesture input, these results show how parents use multimodal speech-touch input and raise the possibility that infants use touch cues to segment and map early words.

articles.title: Developmental Changes in Infants’ Ability to Cope with Dialect Variation in Word Segmentation
articles.authors: No authors listed
articles.abstract: Towards the end of their first year of life, infants learn to ignore variation in sounds not present, or not functional, in their ambient language. Specifically, overly specified word representations are thought to give way to others with which learners can cope better with indexical variation, such as voice and affect, which are not relevant to word identity. This developmental change may help infants in their second year to more efficiently process the ambient language and thus make rapid gains in vocabulary. One particular kind of variability that infants must accommodate is that of dialectal accent, since most children will encounter speakers from different regions and backgrounds. In this study, we explore developmental changes in infants’ ability to recognize words in continuous speech by familiarizing them with words spoken by a speaker of their own region (North Midland American English) or a different region (Southern Ontario Canadian English), and testing them with passages spoken by a speaker of the opposite dialectal accent. Our results demonstrate that 12- but not 9-month-olds readily recognize words in the face of dialectal variation.
